4Neural Network Basics

A neural network is many small “weighted sum + activation” parts stacked in layers; it learns by looping forward pass → loss → backprop → update, many times over.

ⓘ Notes
A neural network is many small “weighted sum + activation” parts stacked in layers; it learns by looping forward pass → loss → backprop → update, many times over.

Why it’s designed this way: Instead of writing rules, build a big adjustable function and let data set every knob; the chain rule finds the direction for billions of knobs in one pass. Why such trained networks generalize so well is still largely an empirical finding.

On this page:

🧒 In plain words first

A neural network is built from lots of tiny parts. Each part does one thing: multiply a few numbers by how “important” each is, add them up, and pass the result through a “switch”. Stack thousands of these parts in layers and they can do very complicated things.

Its skill is practised: guess an answer, see how wrong it is, work out which way each knob should turn, turn it a little, and go again.

👆 Tap a box for details
🤏 Pinch or double-tap100%
② Diagram

Go deeper (the full explanation)

Every part of an LLM is built from the simple “weighted sum + activation”, and all its skill comes from one loop: forward → loss → backprop → update. Tap a box for details; the labs below let you try it yourself.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Remember each part in one line: a neuron is the smallest part; many neurons side by side make a layer; many layers stacked make a network. The loss is one score for “how wrong”; backpropagation traces back from the mistake to work out each knob’s “share of the blame”; the learning rate is how far each knob is turned each time.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
🔥 Updated in training🔒 Read-onlyNeuron

The smallest part: multiply each input by a weight, add them up, add a bias, then pass the sum through a “switch” (the activation function).

🔥 Updated in training🔒 Read-onlyA layer (fully connected)

Many neurons side by side, all looking at the same inputs, each giving one number.

🔥 Updated in training🔒 Read-onlyNeural network

Many layers stacked: each layer’s output is the next layer’s input.

Activation

The “switch” or “bend” after the weighted sum: turns straight lines into kinks and curves.

Forward pass

Run the input through every layer to the output, giving the model’s answer (prediction).

Loss function

One number measuring “how far the model’s answer is from the right answer”. Smaller is better.

Backprop

Walk back from the loss and use the chain rule to get every parameter’s gradient: “if it changes a little, how much does the loss change”.

🔥 Updated in training🔒 Read-onlyUpdate (gradient descent)

Every parameter takes a small step against its gradient: new = old − learning rate × gradient.

Computation graph & chain rule

Break the computation into small nodes joined in a graph; to differentiate, walk the graph backwards multiplying each local derivative.

Optimizers: SGD / momentum / Adam

The rule for “exactly how to step once you have the gradient”.

Learning rate

How big each step is. One of the most important hyperparameters.

Note: this is the principle. A real LLM’s “neurons” are exactly these, just with billions of parameters and a more refined structure (attention, residuals, normalization).
🧪 LabSample data

🧪 One neuron: drag the weights and watch it draw a line

🧒 In plain words first

One neuron is like a vote: x₁ and x₂ are two inputs, w₁ and w₂ say how much each input’s vote counts, and b (the bias) is the bar to clear. Drag them and watch the dividing line turn and move.

  • Why it works this way: A neuron is just “weighted vote + threshold + switch”.
  • On a 2D plane, the place where its output equals 0.5 is a straight line: the weights set the line’s direction, the bias shifts it.
👀 Try:
  • Drag w₂ to 0 and the line turns vertical (only x₁ counts)
  • change the bias and it shifts
  • switch to step and the edge turns hard (no “how sure”).
  • Whatever you do it stays one straight line—separating an XOR pattern needs several neurons in a network (see the “tiny network” lab below).
🧪 Lab

🧪 Activation functions: shape, slope and vanishing gradients

🧒 In plain words first

The “switch” (the activation function) bends straight lines. z is the number going into the switch. Compare the shapes; with many layers stacked, some switches make the “how to fix it” signal fade away as it is passed back.

  • Why it works this way: Without a bend, any number of layers equals one (linear of linear is linear).
  • But the bend’s slope also decides whether gradients get back: backprop multiplies by the slope at every layer, and stacking layers with slopes below 1 makes the gradient vanish.

Why must there be a nonlinearity?

👀 Try:
  • Pick sigmoid and drag layers to 20: less than a millionth of the gradient survives, so early layers barely learn.
  • Switch to ReLU (with positive input) and it stays 1. Tick “remove activation”: 6 neurons in two layers still draw a straight line.
🧪 LabSample data

🧪 Backprop step by step: the computation graph and the chain rule

🧒 In plain words first

Watch one round of training step by step: x is the input, w the weight, b the bias. First work forward to the answer and the error L, then work back to how much w and b should each change, then change them a little.

  • Why it works this way: Each node only needs its own local derivative.
  • Walking back from the loss, each node multiplies “the gradient from upstream” by its local derivative and passes it on—that is the chain rule, and one backward pass gives every parameter’s gradient.
👀 Try:
  • Keep pressing “Next”: forward computes z, a, L, backward gives ∂L/∂w and ∂L/∂b, then the update.
  • Go several rounds and watch the loss shrink.
  • Set w to 2 and x to 2: z is large, σ′ is almost 0 and the gradient nearly vanishes (sigmoid saturation).
🧪 LabToy landscape

🧪 Gradient descent downhill: SGD / momentum / Adam and the learning rate

🧒 In plain words first

Watch three ways of “walking downhill” race on the same ground: plain step by step, walking with momentum, and a walk that adjusts its own step size (Adam). Also try what happens when the steps are too big.

  • Why it works this way: The gradient only says which way is steepest underfoot, not how far to go.
  • In a narrow valley plain SGD zig-zags
  • momentum’s inertia cancels the back-and-forth
  • Adam also scales each direction’s step by its slope.
  • Too big a learning rate overshoots the bottom and can climb ever higher.
👀 Try:
  • Tap “About right” and play: SGD zig-zags in the valley, momentum rushes ahead, Adam goes straightest.
  • “Too small”: barely moves
  • “Too big”: oscillates
  • “Diverges”: flies off the map.
  • Switch to “Two pits” and tap different starting points: starting on the right it often gets stuck in the shallow pit—gradient descent only sees the ground underfoot.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

The examples are split three ways, like homework, quizzes and the final exam: homework is for learning; quizzes check progress and say when to stop; the final is taken only once, at the end, to show real skill. Each improvement uses a small stack of homework; going through all of it once is one epoch.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
Mini-batches & epochs

Each update uses only a small batch of examples; one pass over all the data is an epoch.

Train / validation / test sets

Split data three ways: one to learn from, one to tune settings and decide when to stop, one kept for a single final exam.

Train 70%Val 15%Test 15%
B1B2B3B4B5B6B7B8

The training set is cut into mini-batches: each batch → gradient → one update; all 8 batches = 1 epoch.

One epoch = using the whole training set once, in mini-batches. Each mini-batch gives one average gradient and one parameter update. The validation set is looked at but never learned from, to pick settings and decide when to stop; the test set is used once at the very end.

LLM data is so large it is usually seen about once, so the memorization risk differs from small models; but benchmark questions leaking into training data (contamination) still inflate scores.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Signals pass from layer to layer like a game of telephone: if everyone speaks a bit louder, after dozens of people it becomes shouting; if everyone speaks a bit softer, it fades to nothing. So the knobs start at sensible sizes, and each layer turns the “volume” back to normal.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
Initialization

The small random numbers given to every weight before training starts.

🔥 Updated in training🔒 Read-onlyNormalization (basics)

Pull a layer’s numbers back to a standard size so they don’t keep growing or shrinking.

Weights too big and the signal grows at every layer, exploding after dozens; too small and it fades to zero. Initialization scales the starting point by layer width; normalization recalibrates every layer throughout training.

🧪 LabSample data

🧪 Train a tiny network: decision boundary, overfitting and early stopping

🧒 In plain words first

Train a small network to separate two kinds of dots. Too few neurons and it cannot learn; too many with little data and it memorises the noise, then fails on new points. See when it is time to stop.

ⓘ Sample data: random 2D points

  • Why it works this way: One neuron can only draw a straight line
  • with a hidden layer each neuron draws one line and the output combines them, bending the boundary into any shape.
  • But with too many neurons and too little data it memorizes the noise too—training error keeps falling while unseen test points get worse.
👀 Try:
  • Pick “XOR” with 1 hidden unit → only a straight line, cannot learn
  • set 4 → it learns.
  • Tap “Overfitting demo” (little data, lots of noise, 16 units) and train long: filled training points are nearly all right, hollow test points get worse, and the purple line below marks the best validation moment—that is when to stop early.
  • Then set L2 to 0.01 or turn on dropout and the boundary smooths out.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

A student who only memorises answers is stuck on a new question. “Regularisation” is the set of tricks against memorising: keep the knobs from going to extremes, let some neurons rest at random during practice, stop when the quiz scores get worse, and give more varied examples.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
Regularization

Ways to discourage rote memorization: L2 weight decay, dropout, early stopping, more data.

Dropout

During training, randomly switch off part of the neurons (say half) at every step; at use time all are on.

Four common tricks: L2 weight decay (prefer small weights), dropout (randomly switch off neurons), early stopping (stop when validation gets worse), and more or augmented data. All of them reward “simpler, smoother explanations”; which works best is mostly found by experiment.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

A network for pictures slides a small magnifying glass all over the image: the same glass looks for the same pattern everywhere, like an edge or a corner. Layer by layer the patterns build up: edges → textures → parts → whole things. That means far fewer numbers to learn, and a cat is recognised whether it is top-left or bottom-right.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
🔥 Updated in training🔒 Read-onlyConvolutional network (CNN)

Slide one small “filter” (kernel) across the image to find patterns, combining layer by layer: edges → textures → parts → objects.

🔥 Updated in training🔒 Read-onlyRecurrent neural network (RNN)

Reads one word at a time, updating a “memory” (hidden state) after each, then carries it to the next word.

🔥 Updated in training🔒 Read-onlyLSTM

An RNN with “gates”: switches decide what to keep in memory, what to forget and what to output.

🔥 Updated in training🔒 Read-onlyWord vectors

Each word gets a list of numbers (a vector); words with similar meanings get nearby vectors.

A fully connected layer links every pixel to every neuron, so a 1000×1000 image needs hundreds of millions of weights in the first layer alone. Convolution slides one small 3×3 window across the image, reusing the same weights everywhere: orders of magnitude fewer parameters, and “a cat ear top-left or bottom-right” is recognized either way.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Older recurrent networks are like one person reading a book: word by word, squeezing everything into one small notebook, so by the end the beginning is fuzzy, and nobody can share the reading. A Transformer reads all the words at once, and any two words can “talk” directly, so it is much faster and remembers far-away parts.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
👆 Tap a box for details
🤏 Pinch or double-tap100%

An RNN reads one word at a time, squeezing what it has read into one “memory” vector; the LSTM adds gates and a “memory conveyor belt” so it remembers longer.

  • Parallelism: an RNN’s 100th word waits for the first 99; a Transformer computes all words at once, keeping the GPU busy and training far faster.
  • Long range: in an RNN the 1st word needs 99 steps to reach the 100th, and information and gradients fade on the way; attention connects any two words in one step.
  • No single bottleneck vector: attention can look back at every word’s own vector instead of compressing the whole passage into one fixed-size memory.
The price: attention’s cost grows with the square of the length, so long contexts have revived “memory-style” designs such as linear attention and state-space models—the RNN idea has not fully disappeared.
🧪 LabToy data

🧪 Word-vector space: neighbours and analogies

🧒 In plain words first

Each word is a dot on the map, and words with similar meanings sit close together. A − B + C means “start at A, take away B’s meaning, add C’s”; see which word the arrow lands next to (the positions are an illustrative layout).

ⓘ Toy data: hand-placed 2D illustration

  • Why it works this way: Training pulls together words that appear in similar contexts, so “similar” becomes “close”, and some “relations” become “directions”.
  • Real word vectors have hundreds to thousands of dimensions
  • this is a 2D illustration with hand-placed coordinates, not a real model’s output.
👀 Try:
  • Tap any word to see its three nearest neighbours.
  • Then try the three analogy presets: where does the arrow A − B + C land?
  • In real models analogies only hold roughly, and vectors also pick up biases in the data.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

The idea of neural networks is over eighty years old. Many of the ideas came early; they suddenly got strong after 2012 because three things finally came together: huge amounts of data, fast enough graphics chips, and tricks that let very deep networks train.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
1943McCulloch & Pitts propose a mathematical model of the artificial neuron
1958Rosenblatt’s perceptron: the first neural network that learns from examples
1969Minsky & Papert show a single-layer perceptron can’t learn XOR; the field goes quiet
1986Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams popularize backpropagation; multi-layer networks become trainable
1989–1998LeCun’s convolutional nets read handwritten digits (LeNet), used on bank cheques
1997Hochreiter & Schmidhuber introduce the LSTM
2012AlexNet wins ImageNet by a wide margin with GPUs + ReLU + dropout; deep learning takes off
2013word2vec: word vectors show “king − man + woman ≈ queen”
2014Sequence-to-sequence translation, early attention, the Adam optimizer, GANs
2015Residual networks (ResNet) and batch normalization make 100+ layer networks trainable
2017The Transformer: “Attention Is All You Need”, recurrence removed
2018GPT-1 and BERT: pre-train on huge text, then fine-tune
2020GPT-3 (175B parameters) shows few-shot “learning from a few examples”
2022Nov 30: ChatGPT launches, tuned with instructions and RLHF
Many key ideas are decades old; the post-2012 boom came from three things arriving together: big data, GPU compute, and the tricks that make deep networks trainable (ReLU, good initialization, normalization, residuals).
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

How can a network make new things? One way: learn to squeeze a picture into a few numbers and rebuild it; then pick some numbers at random and rebuild a brand-new picture. Another is like a contest between a forger and a bank teller: one network makes pictures, the other tells real from fake, and both get better together.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

To be more exact…“Pick some numbers at random” needs a condition: only when training deliberately pulls those numbers towards a standard shape, as a VAE does, do random picks mostly rebuild into decent pictures; a plain autoencoder cannot. The forger-and-teller contest can also get out of balance, so the forger ends up drawing the same picture every time (mode collapse).

Autoencoders, VAEs and GANs: two ideas: compress then reconstruct, or train two networks against each other.

  • VAE: the encoder outputs a mean μ and standard deviation σ, and z = μ + σ·ε (ε is standard normal noise), so gradients pass through the sampling. The objective is reconstruction error plus a KL term pulling z towards a standard normal, so any sampled z decodes to something plausible.
  • GAN: G tries to fool D, D tries to tell real from fake. At the theoretical optimum G’s distribution equals the data’s and D can only guess 1/2.
  • Risk: if G and D fall out of sync, G turns many noise vectors into the same image (mode collapse).

Sources: Kingma & Welling 2013, Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (arXiv 1312.6114) · Goodfellow et al. 2014, Generative Adversarial Nets (arXiv 1406.2661) · Overseas academic / legal site: access from mainland China not tested, and no verified mainland mirror found
